name: Business analyst
summary: Business analyst interviews usually test how you turn a vague business need into clear requirements, and how you work between business teams and developers. Candidates commonly report questions on gathering and documenting requirements, process mapping, user stories and acceptance criteria, plus SQL or Excel for some roles and a case on improving a process.
rounds: Aptitude, Excel or SQL test for some roles, often in campus hiring
Functional interview: requirements, documentation, process mapping and methods
Case or scenario round: analyse a business problem or improve a process
Hiring manager round on past projects and work with stakeholders
looks_for: Asking good questions to find the real need behind a request
Clear requirements: user stories, acceptance criteria and process flows
Bridging business and technical teams without losing detail
Handling stakeholders who want different things
Attention to detail and edge cases

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found that what a stakeholder asked for wasn't what they needed.
covers: The original request
The questions or analysis that showed the underlying need
What was built instead, and how it helped

questions.text: Describe a time requirements changed late in a project. How did you handle it?
covers: What changed, and why
How you assessed the impact with the team
How the change was agreed and documented

questions.text: Tell me about a time developers built something different from what the business expected.
covers: Where the gap came from, including your own part in it
How you resolved it
What you changed in how you write or review requirements

questions.text: Tell me about a recommendation you made that was backed by data.
covers: The problem and the data you used
Your analysis and what you recommended
What was decided, and the result

questions.text: How do you gather requirements for a new system? Talk me through your approach.
covers: Identifying stakeholders and the people who'll use the system
Interviews, workshops, watching people work, reviewing existing documents
Confirming and prioritising requirements, for example with MoSCoW

questions.text: Talk me through a user story, with acceptance criteria, for a customer resetting a forgotten password.
covers: The 'As a…, I want…, so that…' form
Acceptance criteria in given-when-then form, including an unknown email and an expired link
Non-functional points such as how long the link lasts and security checks

questions.text: What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give examples.
covers: What the system does versus how well it does it
Examples: create an invoice, versus load a page within two seconds
Why non-functional requirements are often missed, and how you catch them

questions.text: How would you map and improve a slow, manual approval process?
covers: Mapping the current process with the people who actually do it
Finding delays, rework and steps that add nothing
Designing the new process, its benefits, and how you'd measure them

questions.text: What documents does a business analyst produce, and when would you write a BRD rather than user stories?
covers: BRDs, functional specs, process maps, use cases and user stories
Formal documents for Waterfall or regulated work; user stories for Agile teams
Keeping documents short enough that people read them

questions.text: What is a gap analysis, and how would you carry one out?
covers: The current state, the desired state and the gap between them
How you gather evidence for each
Turning the gaps into prioritised actions

questions.text: Two departments want opposite changes to the same screen. What do you do?
covers: Understanding each side's goal and the cost of each option
Bringing data or user evidence into the discussion
Escalating with a clear recommendation if they still can't agree

questions.text: How would you use SQL or Excel to check whether a new process actually saved time?
covers: Defining the measure, such as time from request to approval
Comparing before and after, and filtering out unusual cases
A pivot table or a GROUP BY query, and presenting the result simply

questions.text: What is user acceptance testing, and what is the business analyst's role in it?
covers: Business users checking the system meets their needs before release
Preparing test scenarios from the acceptance criteria
Tracking issues to closure and getting sign-off

questions.text: The sales team says the new CRM is 'too slow to use'. How would you investigate?
covers: Clarifying what slow means: the system's speed, or too many steps
Watching people use it and checking usage data
Proposing fixes and agreeing priorities with the team

questions.text: Explain a use case diagram and a swimlane process diagram, and when you'd use each.
covers: Use case diagrams: the people or systems involved and what they do with the system
Swimlanes: process steps by role, showing hand-offs
Choosing the one that answers your audience's question

questions.text: Why do you want to be a business analyst?
covers: What you enjoy: solving problems, working with people, connecting teams
An example from your studies or work
The domain you'd like to work in

questions.text: Which industry interests you most, and what do you know about how it works?
covers: An industry such as banking, retail or healthcare, with a reason
A basic picture of how it makes money and its main processes
How your skills apply there

tips: Ask clarifying questions before answering any scenario; for a business analyst, the questions are part of the answer.
Bring a sample user story or process map you've written (with nothing confidential) and explain your choices.
Learn basic SQL and Excel pivot tables; many analyst roles test them even when the job title doesn't say so.
Use one industry consistently in your examples; it shows depth.
In stakeholder stories, show how you kept the relationship working, not only whose view won.
